title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
summary: Return the node values level by level, left to right.
statement:
Return the values of the tree level by level: a list for each level, from the root level down, with each level's values from left to right.

The tree is given in level order, with `null` marking a missing child. Visit it with a queue, processing one whole level at a time.
hints: Use a queue: nodes come out in the order they went in, which is level by level.
At the start of each level, the queue holds exactly that level. Record its size before you start.
Pop that many nodes into the current level's list, pushing their children for the next level.
explain: The root 3 is alone on the first level, 9 and 20 form the second, and 15 and 7 (the children of 20) form the third. So the answer is `[[3],[9,20],[15,7]]`.

title: Average of Levels in Binary Tree
summary: Return the average value of the nodes on each level, top to bottom (answers within 10^-5 are accepted).
statement:
Return the average of the node values on each level of the tree, from the top level down.

Answers within `10^-5` of the exact value are accepted.

Process the tree one level at a time with a queue, summing the values on each level and dividing by how many there are. Use a wide enough type for the sums.
hints: This is a level-order traversal where you only keep one number per level.
Process the queue one level at a time, adding the values and counting the nodes.
Values can be as large as 2³¹ − 1, so add them in a long or a double to avoid overflow.

title: Minimum Depth of Binary Tree
summary: Return the number of nodes on the shortest path from the root down to a leaf.
statement:
Return the minimum depth of the tree: the number of nodes on the shortest path from the root down to a leaf (a node with no children). An empty tree has depth 0.

Careful: a node with only one child is not a leaf, so the path has to continue down that child. A level-by-level search can stop at the first leaf it meets.
hints: A node with only one child is not a leaf. That is the trap in a simple 1 + min(left, right).
Breadth-first search finds the nearest leaf first: return the current depth at the first leaf you pop.
In a recursive version, if one child is null, return 1 + the depth of the other child.
explain: Node 9 has no children, so it is a leaf only two nodes from the top (3 → 9). The other leaves, 15 and 7, are three nodes down, so the answer is 2.

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
summary: Standing to the right of the tree, return the values you see from top to bottom (the last node of each level).
statement:
Imagine standing to the right of the tree. Return the values of the nodes you can see, from top to bottom: on each level, the rightmost node.

A node hidden on the left can still be visible if nothing is to its right on that level: in `[1,2,3,4]` the view is `[1,3,4]` because 4 is the only node on the third level.
hints: The visible node on each level is the last one on that level, even if it sits in the left subtree.
Do a level-order traversal and record the last node popped on each level.
Alternatively, run a DFS that visits right before left and records the first node it reaches at each new depth.
explain: The rightmost node on each level is 1 on the first, 3 on the second, and 4 on the third (it sits further right than 5). So you see `[1,3,4]`.

title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
summary: Return the values level by level, alternating left-to-right and right-to-left (starting left-to-right).
statement:
Return the values level by level, alternating direction: the first level left to right, the next right to left, and so on.

Collect each level in the normal left-to-right order, then reverse every other level (or fill it from the back) before adding it to the answer.
hints: Start with an ordinary level-order traversal.
Keep a flag that flips after each level.
Either reverse the level's list on alternate levels, or build it with a deque, adding to the front on right-to-left levels.
explain: The first level [3] is read left to right, the second is read right to left as [20, 9], and the third left to right again as [15, 7]. So the answer is `[[3],[20,9],[15,7]]`.

title: Find Largest Value in Each Tree Row
summary: Return the largest value on each level of the tree, top to bottom.
statement:
Return a list with the largest value on each level of the tree, from the top level down. An empty tree gives an empty list.

Values can be negative, so start each level's maximum from the first node on it rather than from 0.
hints: Visit the tree level by level and keep the maximum of each level.
Start each level's maximum at the first node's value (or Integer.MIN_VALUE) and update it as you pop nodes.
Values can be Integer.MIN_VALUE itself, so make sure a level of only those values still reports it correctly.
explain: The levels are [1], [3, 2] and [5, 3, 9]. Their largest values are 1, 3 and 9, so the answer is `[1,3,9]`.

title: Populating Next Right Pointers in Each Node
summary: In a perfect binary tree, set each node's next pointer to the node on its right on the same level (null at the end). The judge prints each level via next pointers, ending each level with "#".
statement:
The tree is perfect: every internal node has two children and all leaves are on the same level. Each node has an extra pointer `next`. Set every node's `next` to the node to its right on the same level, or to `null` for the last node of a level.

Return the root. The judge prints each level by following `next` pointers, ending every level with `#`.
constraints: The tree is a perfect binary tree
hints: A level-order traversal with a queue works: link each node to the next one popped on the same level.
For O(1) extra space, use the next pointers of the level you have already connected to walk across it.
For each node on a level: node.left.next = node.right, and if node.next exists, node.right.next = node.next.left. Then move down to the leftmost node of the next level.
explain: After linking, 1 points to nothing, 2 points to 3, and 4 → 5 → 6 → 7 on the bottom level. Read level by level with "#" marking the end of each level, that is `["1","#","2","3","#","4","5","6","7","#"]`.

title: Maximum Width of Binary Tree
summary: A level's width is the distance between its leftmost and rightmost non-null nodes, counting the null positions in between as if the tree were complete. Return the maximum width.
statement:
The width of a level is the number of positions between its leftmost and rightmost non-null nodes, inclusive, counting the empty positions in between as if the tree were a complete binary tree.

Return the maximum width over all levels. The answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer.
hints: Give every node a position number as in a heap: the root is 0, the children of i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.
Do a level-order traversal carrying these positions. A level's width is last position − first position + 1.
Positions double every level and can overflow. Subtract the level's first position from each position before computing the children.
explain: The bottom level holds 5, 3, a missing node, and 9. Counting from the leftmost node (5) to the rightmost (9), including the gap, gives width 4, the largest of any level.
